Law 25 assented 2021-09-22; phased entry into force: 2022-09-22 (privacy officer, incident reporting, biometrics disclosure), 2023-09-22 (main obligations: consent, privacy policy, PIAs, transparency, automated decisions, private right of action, penalties), 2024-09-22 (data portability). Sources differ on exact phase contents; original Act P-39.1 dates from 1993/1994.
Not generally covered (living individuals); an enterprise may communicate information to a deceased person's spouse or close relatives where it helps their grieving process (added by Law 25)
Information may be released without consent for study or research purposes after a privacy impact assessment and written agreement (s.21-21.0.2)
No specific genetic rule; falls under sensitive information (medical or intimate) requiring express consent (s.12, 12 para 2)

Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Alberta (OIPC)
Individuals in Alberta whose personal information is handled by private-sector organizations
Private-sector organizations in Alberta: corporations, unincorporated associations, trade unions, partnerships, individuals acting in a commercial capacity (s.1)

Consent for collection, use and disclosure with reasonable purposes (s.7-8, 11-19); access and correction rights (s.24-25); mandatory notification of the Commissioner of incidents posing a real risk of significant harm (s.34.1)
Personal information; employee personal information
Retain only as long as reasonable for legal or business purposes (s.35)
Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Alberta (OIPC)
Offence fines up to CAD 100,000 for organizations and CAD 10,000 for individuals (s.59); Commissioner has binding order-making power but no administrative penalties
Personal or domestic use, journalistic/artistic/literary purposes, public bodies under FOIP, health information under the Health Information Act (s.4)

Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner for British Columbia (OIPC BC)
Individuals in British Columbia whose personal information is held by private organizations

Private organizations (corporations, partnerships, unincorporated associations, trade unions, trusts, not-for-profits) collecting, using or disclosing personal information in BC; federal PIPEDA prevails for federal works
Consent and reasonable purposes (s.6-8, 10-12, 14-18); access and correction rights (s.23-24); reasonable security safeguards (s.34); no mandatory breach notification in the current Act
Personal information; employee personal information
Retain for at least one year after use for decisions about the individual; destroy or anonymize when no longer needed for legal or business purposes (s.35)
Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner for British Columbia (OIPC BC)
Offence fines up to CAD 100,000 for organizations and CAD 10,000 for individuals (s.56); Commissioner can investigate, audit and issue binding orders but has no administrative monetary penalty power
Personal or domestic purposes, journalistic/artistic/literary purposes, public bodies under FOIPPA, business contact information (s.3)
